title: Where death is, I am not
hook: Epicurus: death is nothing to us, for when we are, death is not (Letter to Menoeceus)

segments.voice: Yesterday: autarkeia, the self-sufficiency that makes you hard to frighten. Your line was hard to frighten. What did your plain meal taste like? Day six hundred fifty-two.

On some old Roman gravestones, archaeologists keep finding the same short line, sometimes just as initials. In Latin it runs: I was not, I was, I am not, I don't care. It sounds bleak at first. Then strangely calm. Whoever carved it was likely echoing a teaching from the Garden, an argument Epicurus made to his friend Menoeceus about the thing people fear most. The argument fits in a single sentence, and people are still arguing with it. Today: Lucretius.
screen: `I WAS NOT, I WAS, I AM NOT.` → `I DON'T CARE.` → `THE ARGUMENT FROM THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: First, the argument. In the Letter to Menoeceus, Epicurus says: get used to thinking that death is nothing to us. Why? Because everything good and bad is a matter of feeling, and death is the end of feeling. So while we are, death is not here; and when death is here, we are not. It never meets us. Second, the fear it's aimed at. Epicurus wasn't trying to make dying painless, or losing someone easy. He was aiming at a specific dread: the fear of being dead, of some terrible state afterward. If there's no one there to suffer it, he says, there's nothing to fear in it. Third, a later echo. The Roman poet Lucretius, an Epicurean, added a second picture: think of all the time before you were born. It didn't trouble you. The time after you die, he said, is a mirror of it. Fourth, honesty about where people stand. Epicurus's argument depends on his belief that the soul is made of atoms and scatters at death. Many people, in many traditions, believe something continues after death, and find comfort there instead. Others, especially in the Garden's tradition, find comfort exactly here, in nothing to fear. The path doesn't settle that. It notices that thoughtful people for two thousand years have found this one sentence steadying, or troubling, or both. Either way, it asks something useful: is it death you fear, or something about living, like unfinished things, or leaving people behind? Those, at least, can be worked on today.
screen: `WHILE WE ARE, DEATH IS NOT.` · `NOT DYING: THE DREAD OF BEING DEAD.` · `LUCRETIUS: THE MIRROR OF BEFORE.` · `WHAT DO YOU REALLY FEAR?` · then, large: `WHERE DEATH IS, I'M NOT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe gently. If this topic is heavy for you today, you can simply follow the breath instead. If you're willing, hold Epicurus's sentence lightly: while I am, death is not; when death is, I am not. Don't decide whether you agree. Just notice what it stirs. Calm? Resistance? Something else? Then ask, quietly: underneath, what am I actually afraid of? Let the answer come in its own words, and notice whether it's something you can tend to while you're here. The bell holds the time.
Lucretius. The Epicurean poet who pictured the time after death as a mirror of all the time before you were born. Today's word.

howItsDone: Epicureans have long repeated the teaching that death is nothing to us as a remedy for the fear of being dead, and the Latin epitaph 'I was not, I was, I am not, I don't care' appears on many Roman tombs.

fork.reveal: Epicurus says death never meets us: while we are, it isn't; when it is, we aren't. many people, from many traditions, answer differently.

original.note: Greek: death is nothing to us. Epicurus's words, in the Letter to Menoeceus and the second Principal Doctrine.

trapdoor: what you thought: "death is nothing to us" is just bravado.
what it means: a precise argument: death is the end of feeling, so it can never be suffered by the one who has died.
what a scholar hears: Principal Doctrine 2 compresses the argument; Lucretius adds the symmetry argument in book three of On the Nature of Things, and philosophers still debate whether it works.

sources.work: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things

notes: The epitaph non fui, fui, non sum, non curo (often abbreviated NFFNSNC) appears on Roman tombstones; the link to Epicureanism is common but not certain ('likely echoing'). Confirm.
Letter to Menoeceus 124–125 paraphrased. Confirm. Menoeceus's age is not known; 'young friend' removed in review.
Greek of PD 2 and Menoeceus 124: ὁ θάνατος οὐδὲν πρὸς ἡμᾶς. Confirm accents.
Lucretius symmetry argument: De Rerum Natura 3.972–977. Confirm line numbers.
